title: How do planes fly?
subtitle: The physics of flight
subject: sciences
description: A plane weighing several hundred tons flies. It is not magic: it comes down to the shape of a wing, speed, and forces that balance out.

hero.hook: Heavier than a truck, and still it stays in the air. Here is how.

blocks.text: A big airliner can weigh **hundreds of tons**. How can anything that heavy stay up in the air? The answer lies in the shape of the wings and the speed of the plane.
Four main forces are at work: **thrust** (forward), **drag** (the braking pull of the air), **weight** (downward) and **lift** (upward).
Seen from the side, a plane's wing is not flat. The top is more curved than the bottom. When the plane moves fast, the air has to flow around that shape.

blocks.caption: The shape of the wing creates the lift that holds the plane up

blocks.text: The air passing over the top speeds up a little, so its pressure drops. Under the wing, the pressure stays higher. That difference pushes the wing upward, and that push is **lift**. It is usually explained with **Bernoulli**'s principle, named for an 18th-century scientist, and with the fact that the wing also deflects air downward.
Without speed, too little air flows over the wing and there is not enough lift. That is why a plane needs a long runway to take off: the engines have to accelerate it hard enough.
Birds use the same basic idea, since their wings create lift too. But they flap to move forward. A plane moves forward thanks to its engines.
In cruise flight, lift balances weight. Engine thrust balances the drag of the air. The plane then flies at a roughly constant speed.

To climb, the pilot (or the onboard computer) raises the nose a little and adjusts the thrust. To descend, the thrust is usually reduced. To turn, the plane banks to one side using moving parts of the wings, the ailerons.

On landing, the plane slows down. Flaps extend from the wing to add lift at low speed. Then the wheels touch the ground, and the brakes, sometimes helped by thrust reversers, bring the plane to a stop.
A helium balloon floats because it is less dense than air. A plane is not: it is far denser. It flies because it **forces** the air to carry it, thanks to its speed and the shape of its wings.
A plane flies thanks to the **lift** created by its wings moving through the air. Speed is essential: without it, the wing no longer “pushes” hard enough upward to offset the weight.
